questions.question: Why do mathematicians prefer radians over degrees, and what does 1 radian mean geometrically?
questions.solution: 1 radian = the angle subtending an arc equal to the radius — a natural, dimensionless unit (arc/radius). Calculus formulas become clean: d/dx(sin x) = cos x only in radians; in degrees an ugly π/180 factor appears. Radians make angle a pure ratio, tying trigonometry to arc length directly.

questions.question: Why does sin(θ + 360°) = sinθ? Explain with the unit circle.
questions.solution: θ and θ + 360° end at the SAME point on the unit circle — same coordinates (cosθ, sinθ). Trig functions are the coordinates of a point rotating on a circle, so they repeat every full turn: period 360° (2π). All 'periodic' properties of trig functions come from circular motion.

questions.question: Why is sin(A+B) ≠ sinA + sinB? Give a counterexample and state the correct expansion.
questions.solution: Counterexample: A = B = 30°. sin60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.866, but sin30° + sin30° = 1 — not equal. Sine is a function of the ANGLE, not linear in it; the correct expansion sin(A+B) = sinA cosB + cosA sinB comes from rotating a point on the unit circle by B then A. Functions of angles don't distribute.

questions.question: Why is cos(90° − θ) = sinθ? Give the unit-circle reasoning.
questions.solution: The point at angle θ is (cosθ, sinθ); the point at 90° − θ is its REFLECTION in the line y = x — coordinates swapped: (sinθ, cosθ). Since the x-coordinate is cos of the angle: cos(90°−θ) = sinθ. Complementary angles swap the roles of x and y on the circle.

questions.question: Why does sinθ = ½ have infinitely many solutions while a linear equation has one?
questions.solution: The line y = ½ crosses the sine wave TWICE per period, and the wave repeats forever — so solutions come in infinite periodic families: θ = 30° + 360°n or 150° + 360°n. Trig equations must be answered with the general solution (adding the period), not a single value.

questions.question: Explain the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 without using any formula sheet — from first principles.
questions.solution: Place θ on a unit circle: the point is (cosθ, sinθ). Its distance from the origin is the radius, which is 1. Pythagoras gives cos²θ + sin²θ = 1². The identity is the equation of the unit circle, and it holds for every angle because every point on the circle is at radius 1.

questions.question: Why does sin(θ + 360°) equal sinθ, and why can that be seen in the circle?
questions.solution: Adding 360° returns the radius to the same position, so the point (cos, sin) is identical — every coordinate repeats. Periodicity is the circle's closure: one full turn restores the state. The same reasoning gives cos and tan their periods, with tan repeating every 180° because it is a ratio whose signs change together.

questions.concept: Why the sine rule needs a pair
questions.question: Why can you not use a/sinA = b/sinB with two angles and no side?
questions.solution: The sine rule relates a side to the SINE OF THE OPPOSITE angle, so each ratio must pair a known side with a known opposite angle. Two angles with no side gives proportions but no scale — infinitely many similar triangles fit. Scale requires at least one known length; the angles fix shape, not size.
